lust: strong wanting, especially for pleasure matter: the kind of reality that does not know or feel anything, such as hardness, colour or sound meditation: developing the mind; people use this word in many different ways mental: to do with the mind mental factor: something that goes along with each moment of mind and does its own small job, such as feeling or remembering merit: goodness earned by a good deed, which brings a good result later middling: in the middle; neither good nor bad mindfulness: noticing what is really there right now, without forgetting misdeed: a wrong act molasses: thick dark syrup made from sugar momentary: lasting only a moment monk: a man who has left home to follow the Buddha’s rule of life neutral: neither one thing nor the other; in the middle non-self: not a self; not a person; not anyone’s novice: a boy or young man who has begun training to be a monk object: the thing that a moment of mind knows: a colour, a sound, a thought observance: keeping a rule or custom ordained: made a monk perfection: a good quality made as full and strong as it can be precept: a rule of good conduct prospered: to do well; to grow rich purify: to make clean; cleanness reality: something that is really there, not only a name or an idea rebirth: being born again in a new life after this one ends recite: to say a text aloud from memory recklessness: doing things without care for what may happen recluse: a person who lives apart from the world to seek the truth reign: the time during which a king rules rejoice: to be glad repulsion: strong dislike; being pushed away resentment: a sore, angry feeling about being treated badly result: what comes later from a deed done before, as fruit comes from a seed rumour: a story passed from person to person that may not be true sage: a wise person seer: a wise person who sees the truth sensual: to do with the pleasures of the senses: nice sights, sounds, tastes and so on stinginess: not wanting to give or share; meanness

strenuous: needing great effort studiously: carefully, like a hard-working student suffering: pain and trouble; anything that cannot give lasting happiness sympathetic joy: being glad when someone else is happy or does well sympathize: to feel for someone; to share their feelings tolerant: putting up with things and people one does not like torment: to cause great pain to transgressed: to break a rule; to do wrong truthfulness: always telling the truth and keeping to it ultimate: the deepest and most real; what is really there when all the names are taken away unimpeded: not held back by anything universal: found in every one; here, mental factors that come with every moment of mind unshakeable: cannot be shaken or moved untempered: not softened urgency: the feeling that something must be done now, without delay wrong view: a wrong idea about what is real, such as the idea that there is a lasting self wrong-doer: a person who does wrong

Where the stories come from

This book follows The Perfections Leading to Enlightenment by Sujin Boriharnwanaket, translated from the Thai by Nina van Gorkom (Zolag, London, 2007). The whole book can be read free of charge on abhidhamma.org, as a PDF or as an interactive book with questions. The ten chapters here keep to her order, her stories and, as far as a book for young readers allows, her words.

Her book draws on these ancient texts:

The Cariyāpiṭaka (Basket of Conduct), a book of the Khuddaka Nikāya (the Minor Collection) in the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets), and its commentary, the Paramatthadīpanī, written by Dhammapāla. The definitions of the ten perfections (what each one is, what it does, how it shows itself and what it needs) come from this commentary, in the translation by Bhikkhu Bodhi in The All-Embracing Net of Views (Buddhist Publication Society, Kandy). The Jātaka (birth stories) and their commentary. The stories retold here are, by number: Akitti (480), Sona Nanda (532), Susīma (411), Yudañjaya (460), Dasaṇṇaka (401), Saṃvara (462) and Mūgapakkha, the story of Temiya (538), with others named in their chapters. The Ghaṭīkāra Sutta (Middle Length Sayings 81) and its commentary, for Jotipāla. The Mahāniddesa and Cūḷaniddesa (ancient commentaries in the Khuddaka Nikāya), for Piṅgiya, Jatukaṇṇi, the two cities and the hero. The Atthasālinī (The Expositor), the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, the first book of the Abhidhamma, for the pictures of energy and of shame and fear of blame. The Vibhaṅga (Book of Analysis) and its commentary, the Sammohavinodanī (Dispeller of Delusion). The Anumāna Sutta (Middle Length Sayings 15), the Aṅguttara Nikāya (Gradual Sayings) and the Saṃyutta Nikāya (Kindred Sayings), for the suttas quoted.

Where this book quotes a sentence in quotation marks, the words are those of Sujin’s book or of the translation it uses. Everything else is retold in plainer English for readers of about ten years old. Where the ancient texts and modern scholars differ, this book follows the ancient texts.

Answers

Quiz 1 (chapters 1 and 2) 1. (b) a quality that crosses over to the further shore, the eradication of defilements. The perfections are conditions to cross over to the further shore, namely the eradication of defilements. 2. (b) lobha (attachment). The ten perfections have lobha (attachment) as their opposite, so they are developed without expecting a result. 3. (b) freedom from fear, freedom from hostility and freedom from oppression. This is abhaya dāna (the giving of freedom from fear). The same is said of giving up stealing, wrong conduct, wrong speech and intoxicants. 4. (c) weapons, poisons and intoxicants. He does not give things that lead to affliction for others. The other three he does give. 5. He reflects that it is the nature of material possessions to be subject to loss and passing away, and that his possessions are depleted because he did not give in the past. Then he gives whatever he has, limited or abundant. This destroys the fourth shackle to giving. 6. ”… eradicate defilements.” Giving is a perfection only when nothing is expected in return, not even rebirth in a heavenly plane. 7. Sakka came in the guise of a brahmin. Akitti gave him all his sodden Kāra leaves, on three consecutive days. 8. He said he might transgress his vow of asceticism when he saw the appearance of devas (heavenly beings), who are full of glory and delightful to the senses. 9. Hiri (shame) has respect for oneself as its cause. Ottappa (fear of blame) has respect for someone else as its cause. They always arise together. 10. False. The book says the streamwinner observes the five precepts perfectly and cannot transgress them any more. 11. To a brightly shining fire that came into contact with water and was extinguished, so that only black charcoal was left.

Quiz 2 (chapters 3 and 4) 1. (b) not wishing to buy more clothing that only beautifies the body, because what one has is more than sufficient. The book says of the clothing: “we may consider what we have as more than sufficient. In that case we have renunciation in daily life.” Of the extra morsel: “This shows that he does not have renunciation.” Of the warm bath: “we may be attached to the temperature of the water.” 2. Kāma vitakka (thinking about sense pleasures), vyāpāda vitakka (thinking with hate) and vihiṃsā vitakka (thinking about hurting). 3. Nanda kept serving fruit gathered the day before, some of it spoilt or unripe, which would shorten the old parents’ lives. He would not wait for Sona, because he wanted the merit of feeding them for himself. 4. He brought King Manoja of Brahmavaddhana. He had first thought of bringing Sakka, the king of the devas (heavenly beings), but decided that was not fitting. 5. It lets him turn over, so his body gets a little comfort. It gives his mind no ease at all.

6. He taught the Dhamma (the Buddha’s teaching), showing the delight and the misery of sense pleasures, handed the kingdom back to the viceroy, and went to the forest as an ascetic. 7. Dewdrops on the trees, grass tips and spiders’ webs, vanishing as the sun rose. He compared them to all conditioned things, including the lives of all beings. 8. An arrow shot by a skilled archer (sure penetration), a lamp (it lights things up), and a good guide in a forest (no confusion). 9. Sammuti maraṇa (conventional death), samuccheda maraṇa (final death, of the arahant) and khaṇika maraṇa (momentary death). The last one: each moment of citta (consciousness) arises and dies. 10. 1. saying “I shall give this away” (Āyura); 2. really giving the thing away (Pukkusa); 3. giving and never regretting it afterwards (Senaka). Saying is easiest, giving is harder, and giving without regret is hardest of all. That last answer cured the king.

11. False. He asked only for the teaching that makes an end of birth and old age.

Quiz 3 (chapters 5 and 6) 1. (b) effort or endeavour for kusala (good). Viriya (energy) arises with good and bad citta (consciousness) alike. Only effort for kusala (good) can become a perfection. 2. True. The book says that in a lazy person viriya (energy) applies itself to laziness again and again. 3. An old house is strengthened by new pillars: energy supports a person so that good states do not decline. A small army is reinforced by the king and wins: energy does not let the states arising with it retreat. An ox pulling a load out of a marsh presses its knees to the ground and does not drop the load: energy takes up the burden of doing good and does not drop it. 4. (b) sakkāya-diṭṭhi (personality belief, the wrong view that there is a self). The city of bandits is personality belief, the city of peace is nibbāna (the end of all troubles), and the general is the person who develops the mind. 5. He had perseverance; he was valiant; he caused others to persevere; he had great capacities; he was brave and always progressing, not a coward, not frightened; he did not flee. 6. To avoid akusala (bad states) not yet arisen; to overcome akusala (bad states) that have arisen; to develop kusala (good states) not yet arisen; to keep and complete kusala (good states) that have arisen. 7. (b) three times a day, or twice, or at least once; never not at all. Morning, daytime and evening; if not three times then twice; if not twice then once. Not to examine oneself at all is improper. 8. He left at nine in the morning and arrived at two in the afternoon, with no time for lunch. He went to the Dhamma Study and Support Foundation to make a donation, after hearing a radio programme about vipassanā (insight). 9. The youngest of a hundred sons of the King of Vārāṇasī. He never grudged honour to the great sages but fell at their feet with a humble mind; he liked to listen to the wise and had no envy; he did not cut his soldiers’ pay; he protected the merchants so that the city prospered. 10. False. There is only mental energy. Even walking up and down to stay awake happens because of viriya (energy), a cetasika (mental factor). 11. (b) both the unpleasant and the pleasant, so that lobha (attachment) does not arise. Patience is to be developed not merely towards an undesirable object, but also towards a desirable object.

12. Akusala citta (bad consciousness) has probably already arisen. Patience with one’s living conditions, the weather and the place is adhivāsanā khanti (patience with one’s surroundings). 13. The unimpeded weapon of the good; the adornment of those who vanquish the foe; a stream of water extinguishing the fire of anger; a mantra against the poisonous speech of evil people; an ocean in its depth; a panel closing the door to the plane of misery; a staircase to the worlds of the gods and Brahmas. 14. (b) to kill the monkey; he did not give in to anger and spared it. He wanted to keep his sīla (good conduct) pure, and he aspired to become a Buddha. 15. He said that iron beats gold and gold never beats iron, so if Wrong won against Right that day, iron would be as beautiful as gold. Dhamma gave him the way, and the earth opened and swallowed Adhamma. Adhamma was Devadatta. 16. A sheet of gold engraved with the qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, the ten perfections and mindfulness of breathing, packed in box within box. Pukkusāti read it with such joy that he reached jhāna (deep calm of mind); after a month he cut off his hair, put on yellow robes, took a bowl and walked out of his palace to find the Buddha. 17. (b) he had never seen the Buddha, and the Buddha hid his glory and came as an ordinary monk. The Buddha hid his glory like the full moon behind a cloud. Pukkusāti recognised him only while listening to the teaching, and then asked forgiveness for the word “friend”. 18. “Khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā”: patience, endurance, is the highest austerity. 19. The old monk, the father. In the past life the Bodhisatta told him that young boys are like earthen vessels, broken in a moment and impossible to mend, so old men should bear with them patiently.

Quiz 4 (chapters 7 and 8) 1. (b) because when a person speaks a great deal, some deceptive words may be mixed in, like hard uncooked beans among the cooked ones. Some beans cook and some stay hard. Or it may be that everything a person says is true, from the first word to the last. 2. Some devas (heavenly beings) thought he must have become a Buddha himself. He would not accept praise for a quality he did not have, so by those words he showed that he was only a disciple, repeating what he had heard from the Buddha. 3. (b) truth and dhamma, he is pure and he’s a brāhmin. Water does not destroy the roots of evil, so water cannot wash evil away. Truth and the Dhamma make a person pure. 4. He thought that if he denied it the king would believe him, but that in this world there is no surer foundation than truthful speech, and that one who forsakes the truth cannot attain Buddhahood. So he answered that the rumours were true: infatuated by the objects of delusion, he had done wrong. 5. (b) a withered leaf. Nobody is as steady as Mount Sineru; people are withered leaves, and the wind is lobha (attachment), dosa (anger) and moha (ignorance). 6. That for only seven days he had lived the holy life gladly, and for more than fifty years unwillingly. By that truth the poison was destroyed: the boy shook himself, stood up and was well. 7. He heard his father the king pass terrible sentences on four robbers, and he was afraid of doing such deeds himself and being reborn in hell. The next day he remembered his past lives, including a life in the Ussada hell.

8. (c) sixteen years. The nurses tested him in great ways and small from the day he was a month old until he was sixteen. 9. She asked that the kingdom be given to her son. The king refused, so she asked for seven years, then six down to one, then seven months down to one, then half a month, then seven days. The king agreed to seven days. 10. He stepped down, walked up and down, and lifted the chariot by its back as if it were a toy cart. He told the charioteer that a person resting in the shade of a tree does not break its branches: the king was the tree, the prince the branch, and the charioteer the traveller in its shade. 11. 1. sacca (truthfulness); 2. cāga (relinquishment); 3. upasama (calm); 4. paññā (wisdom). Truthfulness, relinquishment, calm and wisdom. Without the four, the book says, the far shore cannot be reached.

12. False. Desiring the end of rebirth is not the same as being steadfast in one’s determination to develop paññā (wisdom).

Quiz 5 (chapters 9 and 10) 1. (b) adosa (non-hate). Mettā (loving-kindness) is adosa (non-hate), the reality that is freedom from anger. 2. If there is true mettā (loving-kindness), a kind deed for a stranger is exactly the same as a kind deed for someone close. When kindness is limited to some people, the citta (consciousness) should be examined to see whether it is kusala (good) or akusala (bad). 3. She did not take him to court, because she did not want to cause unhappiness to anyone, and she said she would pay for the young man’s education. 4. 1. mettā (loving-kindness): a small child; 2. karuṇā (compassion): a sick child; 3. muditā (sympathetic joy): a child growing up well; 4. upekkhā (equanimity): a child who manages his own affairs. Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity, each a support for the next.

5. (b) at the moment he does the deed, because that deed is the cause of his future suffering. “If one sympathizes with him when he receives an undesirable result, one sympathizes too late.” 6. They believe they feel compassion for the snake, but in reality they are disturbed by aversion towards the person who kills it. A disturbed citta (consciousness) is akusala (bad). 7. The Buddha’s teaching, laid down like a thousand goods on the doorstep of every house. Some people open the door and take them in; others never open the door. 8. (b) because a monk receives honour and gifts, and he did not want honour or gain. He lived as a layman with just enough, and the commentary says he was a monk at heart. 9. The skeleton of a corpse, in the cemetery. He said he had even-mindedness towards what is clean and what is dirty, towards happiness and misery, honour and dishonour, and towards the children who tormented him and the wise people who honoured him alike. 10. False. That may be indifference “based on the home life”, which is moha (ignorance), the near enemy of equanimity. 11. Picking and choosing over which people and which days the rules are kept for: keeping the rules of respect only towards one’s parents, or only on the Uposatha (observance) day and not on other days.
